## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Linemen and line inspectors who patrol a utility's poles.
   [HN] "Most utilities solve this problem with foot patrols. Linemen drive out with a clipboard or an iPad, and run
   through a checklist with binoculars to visually confirm everything is in order." [HN] "We're making weatherized,
   hybrid-fixed drones deployed for power utility inspections." → `roles[lineman]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Confirm every pole and line is sound before it fails.
   [HN] "But when the wood starts to rot, or the cotter pin falls out, and a live conductor is dropped on a dead tree on
   a windy day, you get devastating wildfires like the Palisades Fire in LA last year." → `context.job`,
   `statements.problem`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** On an inspection patrol, pole by pole from the ground; and reactive patrols after storms or a
   strange feeder reading.
   [HN] "A lineman can inspect about 50-150 poles per day, yet even the smallest rural electric cooperatives (with about
   ~20 employees) have about 50,000 distribution poles. Clearly the math doesn't work out. As a result, a given utility
   pole is inspected about every 10 years". [HN] "If there's a weird harmonic on a feeder, or a utility needs a rapid
   scan after a storm, we can get on-site within minutes to inspect." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: pole
   inspection patrol`. Author's choice: the window {3, MONTHS} (the research's "monthly cycle" rhythm; spec 120 reads a
   monthly rhythm as 3 MONTHS), Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most": not every lineman is put
   on patrols in a quarter; storm and construction crews may not be).

4. **Which people.** Linemen and inspectors at US electric utilities and rural co-ops.
   [HN] "The U.S. has 7M miles of power lines (enough to go to the moon and back 14 times), and they're aging." [HN]
   "Power utilities are our first customers". → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The utility, per pole or tower inspected.
   [HN] "Our business model is straightforward: inspection as a service. We charge per pole or tower." [HN] "We just
   secured our first major contract and are working out the details of pilots with some big utilities. Our first paid
   flight is mid-April." [LYC1] "If you're interested in piloting our service, reach out to avi@voltairlabs.com" →
   `persona.decision_maker: {role: manager}`. Author's choice: the decider is the utility's inspection manager and the
   tested role "The VP of operations" (with "The co-op board" listed): no public source names a buyer title. Purchase
   friction's tested item "An FAA waiver to fly beyond sight" is from [HN] (avigotskind, a founder): "There's no real
   way around BVLOS regs right now. The real problem is BVLOS + need to recharge." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444564 ;
   the pad safety review is from [HN] "The risk of landing a drone multiple times per day at myriad points around the
   network felt too risky for utility engineers."; the competitive bid is the author's. Commitment's step "pay for a
   pilot on one feeder": [HN] "Our first paid flight is mid-April"; "on one feeder" is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** Fixed-wing drones that live outside and recharge on pads along the lines.
   [HN] "We're making weatherized, long-range (well over 70 miles), fixed-wing drones that can live outside for months
   at a time. They recharge inductively (no connections or moving parts) on stripped-down charging pads that cost a
   couple thousand dollars apiece." [HN] "we use the charging station as an intermediary, dumping the data from our
   drone to a hard drive on the station over a high-speed WiFi link." [HN] (wweissbluth, a founder) "We're collecting
   61MP RGB, LiDAR (DSM DTM) and radiometric thermal for sensors" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444631 .
   The earlier idea, dropped before the HN post: [LYC1] "We build drones that charge directly on transmission lines."
   and [HN] "There's not enough current on distribution lines!" → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`.
   Compatibility (pole tops visible from above — tested; a spot for a pad; findings into the work order system) and
   Adoption friction (review the drone's flags before sending crews — tested; work from a defect list) are the
   author's, from the mechanism's needs. Relative advantage: [HN] "Xcel power found drones to find 60% more defects than
   foot patrols (because of pole-top vantage point)" (less_worry) and the 50-150 poles a day (shorter_time); wording the
   author's.

7. **Price and cost.**
   Price: **the operator's reading.** [HN] gives the unit only ("We charge per pole or tower"); no amount appears in any
   launch-era or later source. The founder's price is set at **$3 to $5 per pole, each**, below the author's estimate
   of the foot patrol's cost per pole, since the founders sell on cost ([HN] "Georgia Power saved 60% on operating
   expenses when they switched to using drones"). Under the engine's `compare` reading the founder's ratio is 30% to
   125% of the cost (CommercialChain.derive).
   Cost, MONEY **$4 to $10 of the pole inspections per pole, each**: author's arithmetic. A lineman's day of 8 hours at
   [BLS] "The median annual wage for electrical power-line installers and repairers was $95,320 in May 2025" ($45.83 an
   hour) is about $367; with a truck and fuel, about $500 a day; over [HN]'s 50-150 poles a day, $3.30 to $10 a pole,
   taken as $4 to $10. The helicopter ($25k a flight) and the drone-in-a-box ($250,000 a box) are left as the founders'
   comparisons in the statement, not folded into the per-pole cost.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (Uncle_Clark) "I work for a utility company and this is brilliant. One other issue that comes into play for
   inspections is right of way." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47446642 ; [HN] (lifis) "Why not just install
   cameras on the poles?" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47452396 ; [HN] (petargyurov, who builds analytics on
   drone and helicopter imagery) "This is a tough problem to solve and for a lot of operators ultimately comes down to
   cost." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444350 . No first-person lineman account exists in the sources.

## Status today

Widened in pitch, same buyer. [YCP] today reads "Autonomous Drones for Earth Observation", with power utilities "the
perfect first customer" ([LYC2] 2026-03-13: "Power utilities are the perfect first customer. ... Voltair can serve
existing multi-billion dollar data markets in road, rail and telecom inspection at 10x lower prices"). [SITE] still sells
utility inspection only ("Voltair | Autonomous Drone Inspection for Electric Utilities"), with charging moved to
"Ground infrastructure at utility substations", and offers a pilot slot. Price today: none public ([SITE], read
2026-10-22: no price or per-pole figure).

- **Any price amount.** Never published, at launch or since; the founder's $3 to $5 per pole is the operator's reading
  (item 7), and the header says so.
- **The cost per pole.** The founders give poles a day, not dollars; $4 to $10 is the author's arithmetic on [BLS].
- **Volumes.** How many poles a utility inspects a year is not asked by Keel (no volume question on `each`); the
  50,000-pole co-op is in the statement only.
- **A buyer title** and every Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment item beyond those quoted in item 5.
- **First-person lineman accounts.** None in the sources; the stories are scripted from the founders' post and the
  thread.
- **Which launch statement is "day one".** [LYC1] (2026-01-23) pitched power-line charging; the entry uses [HN]
  (2026-03-19), where that approach is dropped, as the idea the founders held at launch.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Samuel and Dennis both say what we already do on foot or with linemen is cheap enough that a per-pole drone price is hard to justify, the name says that plainly, and Aiyana's FAA point is a regulatory blocker that rightly stands on its own.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all three answers speak to what a per-pole drone service would be worth.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea, buyer and sending, but screens 24 and 25 still ask how managers should answer and who gets a link under an "Interviews · Sent" kicker, as if the study had already gone out.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 20 and 22 overlap: my first real step is paying for a pilot on one feeder, and then "Offer a pilot?" asks about it again. Screens 3 and 4 also carry the same heading and question.
founder.missing: Volume: nothing asks how many poles or towers a utility would have inspected per year, and I charge per pole, so $3 to $5 means very different things for a 50,000-pole co-op and a big investor-owned utility. Nothing asks for the alternatives I am really priced against either, helicopters at $25k to get off the ground and drone-in-a-box at $250,000 a box, as separate from the foot patrol's cost.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: Mostly a sensible walk from cost to worth to budget to sign-off, but the 'What would take the time in buying Voltair?' screen breaks in as 'One more thing' before the 6-of-6 pilot question, when it belongs with the waiver and sign-off questions or after the final decision.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Whether the drone or AI findings would be accurate enough to replace or reduce ground patrols, including what it misses on a pole and who stands behind a bad call, plus how the results would get into our work-order and asset systems.

screens.instead: What would take the time in getting that FAA waiver through?

screens.why1: After the price, the budget and the sign-off, asking whether I'd actually pay for a pilot is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: A pilot on one feeder is how my trade talks, and I can answer it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I run the inspection programme and decide on pilots like this, so I can answer from what I would actually do.
screens.why4: The three cover the answer, but 'Probably not' has no matching 'Probably yes' and sits close to 'No', and someone like me who'd want to see it work first has only a flat yes to choose from.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose, and the pilot on one feeder is a plain offer with no founder's terms or roles reaching me.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and three options are easy to hold after hearing them once, with 'you'd' turned correctly for speech.
